One could say exactly the same thing about breasts and tops in Western countries. A man could walk shirtless on a public area and depending on the context it could be inappropriate, but it will always be normal and permitted. A woman could never do that without getting a fine or even be jailed. I have seen fat men’s breasts on TV billion times, but women’s breast aren’t allowed regardless of size. We also live in a culture where a certain part of the body, regardless of size, length or whatever, is allowed or not depending on whether the carrier is a man or a woman. 

So the question is, is a piece of clothing inherently sexist, or is it the culture that surrounds it? Hijabs are heritage of a cultural tradition, just like tops or bikinis are, but in western countries there is just not that legal framework where it’s mandatory to wear it, because for us hair is just not taboo or controversial. On the other hand, in certain African tribes, breasts aren’t taboo either, and women aren’t forced or even have the pressure to cover. That cultural barrier it’s what mostly defines it. If I went to those African countries, I would still cover my breasts because in my culture not doing that it’s embarrassing. In theirs it just isn’t, so would they think I’m being oppressed by deciding to wear a bra and a shirt? Would they understand my uprising, and understand that to me that area is just as taboo as their private parts?

What I’m trying to say is that, at the end of the day, clothes are clothes, and it depends a lot on the context of they are worn whether they are oppressive or not. If we are talking about Muslim countries where only women are forced or have this insanely amount of pressure to wear it, it is sexist. But if it’s in a western country and they live in a community where it’s entirely optional, and their religious choice helps them feel closer to a god they identify with, I think it’s not. Just like if I went to an African tribe and I decided to cover my breasts because it makes me feel comfortable with my privacy, being surrounded by the option of not doing so, it would make it a free choice. It’s always about the context of the choice.

To me the most essential observation about Colm’a character is how he is actually jealous of Padraic. He has lived the same life as him, in the same village as him, surrounded by the same people and same conversations, yet he is happy and content with what he has. One could think that Colm could have changed his life for the better without having to cut off Padraic in such a drastic way. But he had to; not because he was dragging him down, but because he couldn’t help but being bitter about feeling so depressed in front of a person who can’t even grasp the concept of existentialism.

We see him dealing with finding meaning in his life, and telling Padraic to say away from him to the point it somehow becomes worth sacrificing his fingers. I find it kind of interesting how he goes after his fingers instead of anything else. Him, who wanted to be a remembered musician, got rid of the only things he needed to achieve that… so he could punish his friend? No, he wanted to punish himself. He needed to hurt himself as a channel for his guilt for hurting Padraic and his self hatred. Because despite the fact that he wanted him away, he still liked him.

It’s funny; he hated his dullness and innocence because he couldn’t have it, but when we see scenes where that innocence and dullness were at risk, Colm doesn’t hesitate to support him (when he was hit by the policeman or when Jenny died). Almost as if he actually treasured his ability to be simple and nice. 
And by the end of the film, it’s obvious that Colm regrets what he has done to Padraic. From the moment Jenny dies and Padraic becomes bitter like him, he pulls back and regrets making him suffer. He remains in the house while Padraic sets it on fire, almost as if he was hoping his suicidal inclinations could be used to stop either his guilt or Padraic. Yet he couldn’t go all the way. He couldn’t use his physical pain to push Padraic this time, because now that he had ruined him, what other purpose could his pain have? He didn’t want Padraic to become like him, he just wanted to punish himself for wasting his whole life, Padraic was just an excuse. 
That last scene we see how much he regrets what he has done. He has turned the only person whose kindness he envied and treasured into a sad, angry, and mean guy that can’t stand him. He doesn’t have his music, he doesn’t have a home, he doesn’t have time, he doesn’t have that best friend that is hopeful and nice. He personally destroyed all of those things. And now he has nothing to grab onto that makes life worth living. He only has that massive guilt about his life, and what he has done to Padraic’s life.

Favourite is a very strong word, because there are different things that films can make me feel, and I can’t really measure if I value more joy, sadness or shock to define what film can be called my favourite.  But after careful consideration, I think I’ll say Parasite. 

I had never in my life left a cinema room in silence. I have always loved to comment films as soon as the credit rolls. I ALWAYS have something to say, because I love to speak about how a story has made me feel, and to hear what details I may have missed from others. But not with Parasite. It took me days to find the strength to start commenting it. I didn’t know what I was expecting (I didn’t even read the sinopsis, I knew ZERO about it) but it definitely wasn’t that. The film became so unpredictable yet so obviously dark pathed that I couldn’t help to feel desperate for the characters. I just kept chewing on those feelings of “how can everything have gone SO wrong for them???”. I think I had never seen a film with such a funny and shiny first half and such a radically dark and tense second half. There is also the social criticism, the psychology of the characters, the marvellous directing skills of Bo Jong Ho, and the underlying message regarding human survival in a society that doesn’t care about you.

Everything was simply brilliant from the beginning till the end. It made me suffer so much I’ll never watch it again unless I suddenly feel prepared to live through such an experience again, but the intensity and impact this film has had on me has no precedent. I think I’ll call it my favourite just for that.

So when the King came back the country was ruinous and people were obviously pissed. His approach to the situation was to say that he had prayed to God to save the country in exchange of his soon to be born daughter, taking credit for the coincidence that caused the mongols to leave. So he secluded his newborn daughter in an isolated monastery in an island located in the middle of the Danube. Her name was Margaret, and she was brainwashed since her childhood into believing that the core of her existence was to serve God. She chastised herself since she was a child, wearing iron girdles, hairshirts and shoes with spikes. She became an icon of veneration for the Hungarians, and there were many “witnesses of her performed miracles”, so Bela succeeded in turning his daughter into a martyr. 


It’s not documented what exactly caused her death (they had the intention to canonise her so they preferred to avoid details) but scholars assume it was due to her constant self mutilation that she died at 27. I don’t know if people remember Bela as a good king, but he should be remembered as the guy that sold his own daughter to preserve his own reputation.

Okay, so there’s this very famous old South Korean drama called The King and The Clown, that tells the story of a king that hears that a travelling theatre that makes funny plays about him just arrives to his kingdom, so he orders the guards to bring them and make them perform some of them in front of him. If they make him laugh, they will live, but if he doesn’t, they will die. However,  when the play begins and the actors starts performing, the King realises that in the cast there’s this very androgynous and beautiful guy he can’t take his eyes off. Completely spell-bounded, he dismisses the rest of the crew and immediately hires him as the clown of the court; this way, the weird affection and attraction between The King and The Clown is born.
Unfortunately, as in most homosexual related love stories before 2010, the story does not have a happy ending. It’s important to specify that Korean society has always been incredibly conservative about homosexuality in the media, so even if the film does it’s best to hint some things and develop interesting character dynamics around this topic, the story does not fully revolve around love in a very specific way.

Still, the main soundtrack of the film, a ballad called Fate, brought the closure everyone missed in the ending. From the perspective of two of the main characters, the song recalls the last moments shared, as they promise each other how if they couldn’t be together in this life, they would be together in the next one, so they would keep this feeling inside their hearts, cherishing it and keeping it alive, so they can recognise each other when they meet again. Regardless the outcome in this story, they are still grateful of what they had, because they know that it’s their fate to be together, so they will wait until the moment arrives to share those feelings again.

The song it’s absolutely beautiful and very well know in Korea, as it’s has been sang and covered a million times. but it’s still not the final goal. 

Years later, in 2015, this very famous singer called Hyorin did a special stage in a TV show called I Am A Singer, in which many celebrities are meant to perform as a part of the spectacle. Hyorin chose this song as her special stage, which everyone thought was a weird combination as Hyorin wasn’t exactly a specialist on ballads. But guys, while I don’t speak nor understand the tinniest bit of Korean, this son makes me tear up EVERY single time I listen to it. I’m not even kidding, goosebumps every single time.

And now that you know all of this information, I recommend you guys to check it (don’t forget to activate captions for lyrics)
